solution:
The hybridisation of a carbon follows from the number of \(\sigma\) bonds it forms: four \(\sigma\) bonds means \(sp^3\), three means \(sp^2\) and two means \(sp\).

\(\text{CH}_2=\text{C}=\text{O}\): the \(\text{CH}_2\) carbon is \(sp^2\); the central carbon carries two double bonds, so it is \(sp\).

\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2\): \(sp^3\) (the \(\text{CH}_3\) carbon), \(sp^2\), \(sp^2\).

\((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CO}\): \(sp^3\), \(sp^2\) (the carbonyl carbon), \(sp^3\).

\(\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCN}\): \(sp^2\), \(sp^2\), \(sp\) (the nitrile carbon).

\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6\): all six ring carbons are \(sp^2\).

Every single bond is one \(\sigma\) bond; a double bond is one \(\sigma\) plus one \(\pi\), and a triple bond one \(\sigma\) plus two \(\pi\).

\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6\): 6 C–C \(\sigma\) + 6 C–H \(\sigma\) = 12 \(\sigma\); 3 \(\pi\).

\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\) (cyclohexane): 6 C–C \(\sigma\) + 12 C–H \(\sigma\) = 18 \(\sigma\); 0 \(\pi\).

\(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2\): 2 C–H \(\sigma\) + 2 C–Cl \(\sigma\) = 4 \(\sigma\); 0 \(\pi\).

\(\text{CH}_2=\text{C}=\text{CH}_2\): 2 C–C \(\sigma\) + 4 C–H \(\sigma\) = 6 \(\sigma\); 2 \(\pi\).

\(\text{CH}_3\text{NO}_2\): 3 C–H \(\sigma\) + 1 C–N \(\sigma\) + 2 N–O \(\sigma\) = 6 \(\sigma\); 1 \(\pi\).

\(\text{HCONHCH}_3\): 1 C–H + 1 C=O \(\sigma\) + 1 C–N + 1 N–H + 1 N–C + 3 C–H (of the methyl) = 8 \(\sigma\); 1 \(\pi\) (the C=O).

In a bond-line formula each line end and each vertex is a carbon; hydrogens on carbon are not shown, and heteroatoms are written explicitly.

Isopropyl alcohol, \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHOH}\): a three-carbon zig-zag with \(\text{OH}\) written on the middle vertex.

2,3-Dimethylbutanal, \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CHO}\): a four-carbon zig-zag whose C-1 vertex carries a doubly bonded \(\text{O}\) and an \(\text{H}\), with a methyl line drawn from the C-2 vertex and another from the C-3 vertex.

Heptan-4-one, \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\): a seven-carbon zig-zag with a doubly bonded \(\text{O}\) on the middle (fourth) vertex.

In each case the longest chain containing the principal functional group is chosen and numbered so that the principal group, then the substituents, get the lowest locants.

(a) A three-carbon chain attached to a benzene ring: **Propylbenzene** (also written 1-phenylpropane).

(b) The nitrile carbon is C-1, so the chain is a five-carbon nitrile with a methyl on C-3: **3-Methylpentanenitrile**.

(c) The longest chain is seven carbons with methyl groups on the 2nd and 5th: **2,5-Dimethylheptane**.

(d) A seven-carbon chain whose C-3 carries both halogens; bromo precedes chloro alphabetically: **3-Bromo-3-chloroheptane**.

(e) The \(-\text{CHO}\) carbon is C-1, so the chlorine is on C-3: **3-Chloropropanal**.

(f) \(\text{Cl}_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{OH}\): the \(-\text{OH}\) carbon is C-1 and both chlorines are on C-2: **2,2-Dichloroethan-1-ol**.

(a) **2,2-Dimethylpentane** is correct. The multiplying prefix 'di' requires a locant for each of the two methyl groups, so '2-Dimethylpentane' is not a valid name.

(b) **2,4,7-Trimethyloctane** is correct. Numbering from the two ends gives the locant sets 2,4,7 and 2,5,7; at the first point of difference 4 is lower than 5, so 2,4,7 is the correct set.

(c) **2-Chloro-4-methylpentane** is correct. Both directions give the same locant set {2,4}, so the tie is broken by giving the lower locant to the substituent that comes first alphabetically — chloro before methyl.

(d) **But-3-yn-1-ol** is correct. The \(-\text{OH}\) is the principal characteristic group and must get the lowest locant, and the suffix order is the unsaturation ('yn') before the principal group ('ol'). 'But-4-ol-1-yne' violates both.

Successive members of a homologous series differ by a \(-\text{CH}_2-\) unit.

(a) Carboxylic acids: \(\text{HCOOH}\), \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\), \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}\), \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}\), \(\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{COOH}\).

(b) Ketones: \(\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3\), \(\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3\), \(\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\), \(\text{CH}_3\text{CO}(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{CH}_3\), \(\text{CH}_3\text{CO}(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{CH}_3\).

(c) Alkenes: \(\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2\), \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2\), \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2\), \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2\), \(\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2\).

(a) 2,2,4-Trimethylpentane. Condensed: \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2\). Bond line: a five-carbon zig-zag with two methyl lines from the C-2 vertex and one from the C-4 vertex. Functional group: **none** — it is a saturated hydrocarbon.

(b) 2-Hydroxy-1,2,3-propanetricarboxylic acid. Condensed: \(\text{HOOCCH}_2\text{C}(\text{OH})(\text{COOH})\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}\). Bond line: a three-carbon chain with a \(-\text{COOH}\) on each of the three carbons and an \(\text{OH}\) on the middle carbon. Functional groups: **three carboxylic acid groups** \((-\text{COOH})\) and **one alcoholic hydroxyl group** \((-\text{OH})\).

(c) Hexanedial. Condensed: \(\text{OHC}(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{CHO}\). Bond line: a six-carbon zig-zag with a doubly bonded \(\text{O}\) on each terminal vertex. Functional groups: **two aldehyde groups** \((-\text{CHO})\).

A functional group is the atom or group of atoms joined to the carbon chain that determines the characteristic chemical properties of the compound.

(a) **Aldehyde** \((-\text{CHO})\), **ether / methoxy** \((-\text{OCH}_3)\) and **phenolic hydroxyl** \((-\text{OH})\), all on a benzene (arene) ring.

(b) **Primary aromatic amine** \((-\text{NH}_2)\), **ester** \((-\text{COO}-)\) and **tertiary amine** \((-\text{N}(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2)\), on a benzene ring.

(c) **Nitro group** \((-\text{NO}_2\)) attached to a **carbon–carbon double bond** \((\text{C}=\text{C})\), which is in turn attached to a benzene ring.

\(\text{O}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{O}^{-}\) is the more stable of the two.

The chapter classifies the nitro group \((-\text{NO}_2)\) as an electron-withdrawing group and alkyl groups such as methyl and ethyl as electron-donating groups. Through its \(-\text{I}\) inductive effect the nitro group draws electron density away from the negatively charged oxygen, dispersing the negative charge over more of the molecule and so stabilising the anion.

In \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^{-}\) the ethyl group instead pushes electron density towards the oxygen \((+\text{I})\), intensifying the negative charge and destabilising the anion.

Hence \(\text{O}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{O}^{-}\) is expected to be more stable.

This is the hyperconjugation effect described in the chapter.

When an alkyl group is attached directly to an atom of an unsaturated (\(\pi\)) system, one of the C–H bonds of the alkyl group can align in the plane of the adjacent \(p\) orbital. The \(\sigma\) electrons of that C–H bond then enter into partial conjugation with the \(\pi\) system, i.e. they are delocalised into it. Electron density therefore flows from the alkyl group into the \(\pi\) system, which is exactly what it means to say the alkyl group acts as an electron donor.

The alkyl group also releases electron density by its \(+\text{I}\) inductive effect, so the two effects reinforce each other. Hyperconjugation is a permanent effect, and the greater the number of C–H bonds available for this overlap, the greater the donation.

In each case the curved arrow starts where a lone pair or a \(\pi\) pair sits and ends where that pair moves to; the positions of the nuclei never change.

(a) \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}\): a lone pair on oxygen moves into the ring, giving structures with \(+\) on oxygen and \(-\) at the ortho and para ring carbons (three such charge-separated contributors, besides the Kekulé forms).

(b) \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2\): ring \(\pi\) electrons move towards the nitro group, giving structures with \(+\) at the ortho and para ring carbons and \(-\) on the nitro oxygen.

(c) \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCHO}\): the \(\text{C}=\text{C}\) \(\pi\) pair shifts to the adjacent bond while the \(\text{C}=\text{O}\) \(\pi\) pair shifts onto oxygen, giving \(\text{CH}_3\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{O}^{-}\) and \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{O}^{-}\).

(d) \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CHO}\): the \(\text{C}=\text{O}\) \(\pi\) pair moves onto oxygen and the ring feeds electron density to the carbonyl carbon, putting \(-\) on oxygen and \(+\) at the ortho and para ring carbons.

(e) \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2\): ring \(\pi\) electrons move to the exocyclic carbon, so the positive charge is delocalised onto the ortho and para ring carbons (three contributors besides the parent).

(f) \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}\,\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2\): the \(\text{C}=\text{C}\) \(\pi\) pair shifts towards the positive carbon, giving \(\text{CH}_3\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2\); the positive charge is shared by the two terminal carbons of the allylic system.

In every case the contributing structures have the same positions of nuclei and the same number of unpaired electrons, and the real molecule is the resonance hybrid, which is lower in energy than any one of them.

A **nucleophile** (Nu:) is a reagent that brings an electron pair to the reactive site of the substrate, i.e. it is nucleus-seeking; the reaction it undergoes is called nucleophilic. A nucleophile attacks the electrophilic centre of the substrate, which is the electron-deficient atom.

Examples: negatively charged ions carrying a lone pair, such as hydroxide \(\text{HO}^{-}\) and cyanide \(\text{NC}^{-}\), and carbanions \(\text{R}_3\text{C}\!:^{-}\); also neutral molecules with a lone pair, such as \(\text{H}_2\ddot{\text{O}}\!:\), \(\text{R}_3\text{N}\!:\) and \(\text{R}_2\ddot{\text{N}}\text{H}\).

An **electrophile** \((\text{E}^{+})\) is a reagent that takes away an electron pair from the reactive site, i.e. it is electron-seeking; the reaction is called electrophilic. An electrophile accepts an electron pair at the nucleophilic (electron-rich) centre of the substrate.

Examples: carbocations such as \(\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}_3\), whose carbon has only a sextet of electrons; and neutral molecules containing a group such as the carbonyl \(>\text{C}=\text{O}\) or an alkyl halide \(\text{R}_3\text{C}-\text{X}\), in which the polarity of the C–X bond puts a partial positive charge on carbon.

(a) \(\text{HO}^{-}\) — **nucleophile**. It carries lone pairs and a negative charge and donates an electron pair.

(b) \({}^{-}\text{CN}\) — **nucleophile**. It brings an electron pair to the electron-deficient carbonyl carbon of propanone.

(c) \(\text{CH}_3\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{O}\) — **electrophile**. Its positively charged carbon has only a sextet of electrons and accepts an electron pair, here from the \(\pi\) electrons of benzene.

[Textbook misprint in part (d), which does not balance in carbon. The reactant \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\) has FIVE carbons (three methyls, a quaternary carbon and the \(-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\)), while the product as printed, \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CBrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\), has SIX. The rearranged five-carbon product this reaction actually gives is \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CBr}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\) (2-bromo-2-methylbutane), formed by a methyl shift to the primary carbocation. The classification the question asks for is unaffected — it is a rearrangement either way, since the carbon skeleton changes and the product is a tertiary rather than a primary bromide — so the answer below stands on the reaction as intended.] The chapter classifies organic reactions as substitution, addition, elimination and rearrangement.

(a) \(\text{HS}^{-}\) replaces \(\text{Br}^{-}\) on the same carbon: a **substitution** reaction (nucleophilic substitution).

(b) \(\text{H}\) and \(\text{Cl}\) add across the \(\text{C}=\text{C}\) double bond and nothing is expelled: an **addition** reaction (electrophilic addition).

(c) \(\text{H}\) and \(\text{Br}\) are lost from adjacent carbons and a double bond is created: an **elimination** reaction.

(d) The carbon skeleton itself changes — the product is a tertiary bromide, not the primary bromide that simple substitution would give — so this is a **rearrangement** reaction.
_note: BOOK DEFECT in part (d): the reactant \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\) has FIVE carbon atoms but the printed product \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CBrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\) has SIX, so the equation is not balanced in carbon. The rearranged five-carbon product would be \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3\). The classification (rearrangement) is unaffected either way. solution:
(a) **Structural isomers.** Both have the molecular formula \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}\) but differ in the position of the carbonyl group along the chain (pentan-3-one and pentan-2-one), so they are position isomers, a kind of structural isomerism.

(b) **Geometrical isomers.** The two structures have the same constitution and the same sequence of bonds but differ in the relative positions of the two deuterium atoms in space: in the first they lie on opposite sides of the \(\text{C}=\text{C}\) bond and in the second on the same side. Rotation about the double bond is restricted, so the two cannot interconvert.

(c) **Resonance contributors.** The positions of the nuclei are identical in the two structures and only the position of an electron pair (and hence of the charge) differs, so they are canonical structures of one and the same species, not separate compounds.

A homolysis is shown with half-headed (fish-hook) arrows and gives neutral species with an unpaired electron; a heterolysis is shown with a full curved arrow and gives ions.

(a) **Homolysis.** The O–O bond breaks so that one electron goes to each oxygen (two fish-hook arrows). The intermediates are **free radicals** — two methoxy radicals \(\text{CH}_3\dot{\text{O}}\). Neither is a carbocation nor a carbanion.

(b) **Heterolysis.** The hydroxide ion removes a proton from a methyl group; a full curved arrow takes the C–H bonding pair onto carbon. The intermediate is a **carbanion** — the carbon left behind carries the electron pair and a negative charge.

(c) **Heterolysis.** A full curved arrow takes the C–Br bonding pair onto bromine, which leaves as \(\text{Br}^{-}\). The intermediate is a **carbocation**, the tertiary \((\text{CH}_3)_3\overset{+}{\text{C}}\), whose carbon has a sextet of electrons.

(d) Here a bond is FORMED rather than cleaved: a curved arrow takes a \(\pi\) pair of the benzene ring to the electrophile \(\text{E}^{+}\). The intermediate is a **carbocation** — the cyclohexadienyl (arenium) cation, in which the positive charge is delocalised over the remaining five ring carbons.

**Inductive effect:** the polarisation of a \(\sigma\) bond caused by the polarisation of an adjacent \(\sigma\) bond. A polar bond induces polarity in the bonds next to it; the effect is transmitted along the chain but falls off rapidly as the number of intervening bonds increases and becomes vanishingly small after about three bonds. It is a permanent effect.

**Electromeric effect:** the complete transfer of a shared pair of \(\pi\) electrons to one of the two atoms joined by a multiple bond, on the demand of an attacking reagent. It is a temporary effect, shown only in the presence of the reagent and annulled as soon as the reagent is removed. Where the two effects operate in opposite directions, the electromeric effect predominates.

Both of the given orders are explained by the **inductive effect**, and neither by the electromeric effect, since neither series involves a multiple bond in the substituent or an attacking reagent.

(a) Chlorine is electron-withdrawing \((-\text{I})\). Three chlorines withdraw more electron density than two, and two more than one, so the negative charge of the carboxylate ion is dispersed best in \(\text{Cl}_3\text{CCOO}^{-}\). The more stable the anion, the stronger the acid, giving the stated order.

(b) Alkyl groups are electron-donating \((+\text{I})\). Going from ethyl through isopropyl to tert-butyl the number of methyl groups feeding electron density towards the carboxyl group increases, intensifying the negative charge on the carboxylate and destabilising it. Acid strength therefore decreases in that order.

(a) **Crystallisation.** Principle: the difference in the solubilities of the compound and of the impurities in a suitable solvent. The impure solid is dissolved in a solvent in which it is sparingly soluble at room temperature but appreciably soluble at a higher temperature; the solution is concentrated to near saturation and then cooled, whereupon the pure compound crystallises out and is filtered off, the impurities remaining in the mother liquor. Coloured impurities are removed by adsorption on activated charcoal, and where the impurities have comparable solubilities the crystallisation is repeated.

(b) **Distillation.** Principle: liquids with different boiling points vaporise at different temperatures. The mixture is heated, the vapours of the lower-boiling component form first, are condensed in a condenser and collected separately; the higher-boiling component follows. Example: chloroform (b.p. \(334\,\text{K}\)) and aniline (b.p. \(457\,\text{K}\)) are easily separated this way. Distillation also separates a volatile liquid from non-volatile impurities.

(c) **Chromatography.** Principle: the components of a mixture applied to a stationary phase are carried along at different rates by a mobile phase, and so become separated. In adsorption chromatography the separation depends on the different degrees to which the components are adsorbed on an adsorbent such as silica gel or alumina; in partition chromatography it depends on their continuous differential partitioning between the stationary and mobile phases. Example: in thin layer chromatography the mixture is spotted on a thin layer of adsorbent on a glass plate and developed in a jar of eluant, the components travelling different distances up the plate; amino acids can be detected on the developed plate by spraying it with ninhydrin solution.
_note: The chapter names an example for distillation (chloroform/aniline) and for chromatography (amino acids with ninhydrin; separation of coloured plant substances, from which the technique takes its name), but it names NO example compound for crystallisation - its section 8.8.2 gives only the principle. The example offered above for chromatography is taken from the chapter's own text.

solution:
The method is **crystallisation** (fractional crystallisation).

The two compounds are dissolved together in the solvent S, chosen so that the compound to be purified is sparingly soluble in it at room temperature but appreciably soluble at a higher temperature. The hot solution is concentrated to give a nearly saturated solution and is then allowed to cool. The less soluble compound reaches saturation first and crystallises out; it is removed by filtration, while the more soluble compound stays behind in the mother liquor along with a small quantity of the first compound.

Because the two solubilities are different, repeating the crystallisation on the crystals so obtained separates the two compounds as completely as required.

**Distillation** separates a volatile liquid from non-volatile impurities, or two liquids whose boiling points differ appreciably. The mixture is boiled at atmospheric pressure, the vapours of the lower-boiling component are condensed and collected first, and those of the higher-boiling component later.

**Distillation under reduced pressure** is used for liquids that have very high boiling points, and for those that decompose at or below their boiling points. A liquid boils at the temperature at which its vapour pressure equals the external pressure, so lowering the pressure over the liquid with a water pump or vacuum pump makes it boil at a temperature well below its normal boiling point, and it distils without decomposing. Glycerol is separated from spent-lye in the soap industry this way.

**Steam distillation** is used for substances that are steam volatile and immiscible with water. Steam is passed through the heated liquid; the mixture boils when \(p = p_1 + p_2\), where \(p_1\) is the vapour pressure of the organic liquid and \(p_2\) that of water. Since \(p_1\) is less than the atmospheric pressure \(p\), the organic liquid distils at a temperature below its own boiling point — in fact just below \(373\,\text{K}\). The distillate is a mixture of water and the compound, which is separated in a separating funnel. Aniline is separated from an aniline–water mixture this way.

In Lassaigne's test the elements nitrogen, sulphur, halogens and phosphorus, which are covalently bonded in an organic compound, are first converted into their ionic forms by fusing the compound with sodium metal:

\(\text{Na} + \text{C} + \text{N} \rightarrow \text{NaCN}\)

\(2\text{Na} + \text{S} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{S}\)

\(\text{Na} + \text{X} \rightarrow \text{NaX}\) (X = Cl, Br or I)

The fused mass is boiled with distilled water to give the **sodium fusion extract**, which is then tested.

**Nitrogen:** the extract is boiled with iron(II) sulphate and acidified with concentrated sulphuric acid. Cyanide first gives sodium hexacyanidoferrate(II); on heating with the acid some \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) is oxidised to \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\), which then gives iron(III) hexacyanidoferrate(II), Prussian blue.

\(6\text{CN}^{-} + \text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow [\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]^{4-}\)

\(3[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]^{4-} + 4\text{Fe}^{3+} \rightarrow \text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]_3\)

**Sulphur:** the extract acidified with acetic acid and treated with lead acetate gives a black precipitate, \(\text{S}^{2-} + \text{Pb}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{PbS}\); with sodium nitroprusside it gives a violet colour, \(\text{S}^{2-} + [\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_5\text{NO}]^{2-} \rightarrow [\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_5\text{NOS}]^{4-}\).

**Halogens:** the extract acidified with nitric acid and treated with silver nitrate gives \(\text{X}^{-} + \text{Ag}^{+} \rightarrow \text{AgX}\) — a white precipitate soluble in ammonium hydroxide for chlorine, a yellowish precipitate sparingly soluble for bromine, and a yellow precipitate insoluble for iodine.

**When nitrogen and sulphur are both present**, sodium thiocyanate is formed instead, \(\text{Na} + \text{C} + \text{N} + \text{S} \rightarrow \text{NaSCN}\), which gives a blood-red colour with \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\), \(\text{Fe}^{3+} + \text{SCN}^{-} \rightarrow [\text{Fe}(\text{SCN})]^{2+}\), and no Prussian blue, since there are no free cyanide ions. If the fusion is carried out with an excess of sodium the thiocyanate decomposes, \(\text{NaSCN} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow \text{NaCN} + \text{Na}_2\text{S}\), and both ions then give their usual tests.

**(i) Dumas method.** The nitrogen-containing compound is heated with copper(II) oxide in an atmosphere of carbon dioxide; the nitrogen of the compound is set free as nitrogen GAS, along with carbon dioxide and water:

\(\text{C}_x\text{H}_y\text{N}_z + (2x + y/2)\,\text{CuO} \rightarrow x\,\text{CO}_2 + (y/2)\,\text{H}_2\text{O} + (z/2)\,\text{N}_2 + (2x + y/2)\,\text{Cu}\)

Any traces of oxides of nitrogen are reduced to nitrogen over heated copper gauze. The gases are collected over aqueous potassium hydroxide, which absorbs the carbon dioxide, and the VOLUME of nitrogen left is measured in a nitrometer. The percentage is then calculated from that volume after correcting it to STP.

**(ii) Kjeldahl's method.** The compound is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid, which converts its nitrogen into ammonium sulphate — so the nitrogen ends up in a COMPOUND, not as free nitrogen. The mixture is then heated with excess sodium hydroxide and the ammonia liberated is absorbed in a known excess of standard sulphuric acid. The acid left unreacted is estimated by titration against standard alkali, and the amount of ammonia, and hence of nitrogen, follows by difference.

So the two differ in principle in what the nitrogen is converted to and in what is measured: Dumas liberates free \(\text{N}_2\) and measures its volume, while Kjeldahl converts the nitrogen to ammonium sulphate and measures it by acid–base titration.

Kjeldahl's method is **not applicable** to compounds containing nitrogen in nitro and azo groups, or nitrogen present in a ring (for example pyridine), because in these the nitrogen is not converted to ammonium sulphate under the conditions used. The Dumas method carries no such restriction.

In each case the element is oxidised to a form that can be precipitated and weighed, and the percentage follows from the mass of the precipitate.

**Halogens — Carius method.** A known mass \(m\) of the compound is heated with fuming nitric acid in the presence of silver nitrate in a sealed hard-glass Carius tube. Carbon and hydrogen are oxidised to carbon dioxide and water, and the halogen forms the corresponding silver halide \(\text{AgX}\), which is filtered, washed, dried and weighed as \(m_1\). Since one mole of \(\text{AgX}\) contains one mole of \(\text{X}\),

percentage of halogen \(= \dfrac{\text{atomic mass of X} \times m_1 \times 100}{\text{molecular mass of AgX} \times m}\)

**Sulphur.** A known mass of the compound is heated in a Carius tube with sodium peroxide or fuming nitric acid; the sulphur is oxidised to sulphuric acid, which is precipitated as barium sulphate by adding excess barium chloride solution. The precipitate is filtered, washed, dried and weighed as \(m_1\). Since \(233\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{BaSO}_4\) contains \(32\,\text{g}\) of sulphur,

percentage of sulphur \(= \dfrac{32 \times m_1 \times 100}{233 \times m}\)

**Phosphorus.** A known mass of the compound is heated with fuming nitric acid; the phosphorus is oxidised to phosphoric acid, which is precipitated as ammonium phosphomolybdate \((\text{NH}_4)_3\text{PO}_4\!\cdot\!12\text{MoO}_3\) by adding ammonia and ammonium molybdate. With \(m_1\) the mass of that precipitate and \(1877\,\text{g}\) its molar mass,

percentage of phosphorus \(= \dfrac{31 \times m_1 \times 100}{1877 \times m}\)

Alternatively the phosphoric acid is precipitated as \(\text{MgNH}_4\text{PO}_4\) with magnesia mixture, which on ignition yields \(\text{Mg}_2\text{P}_2\text{O}_7\) (molar mass \(222\,\text{u}\), containing two phosphorus atoms, \(62\,\text{u}\)), giving

percentage of phosphorus \(= \dfrac{62 \times m_1 \times 100}{222 \times m}\)

Paper chromatography is a type of **partition chromatography**, so its principle is the continuous differential partitioning of the components of a mixture between a stationary and a mobile phase.

A special chromatography paper is used. The paper contains water trapped in it, and this trapped water is the **stationary phase**. A strip of the paper is spotted at its base with the solution of the mixture and suspended in a suitable solvent or mixture of solvents, which is the **mobile phase**.

The solvent rises up the paper by capillary action and flows over the spot. As it does so, each component distributes itself between the trapped water and the moving solvent to a different extent; a component that favours the stationary water is retained more strongly and travels a shorter distance, while one that favours the mobile solvent travels further. The components therefore separate into spots at different heights from the starting position. The developed strip is called a chromatogram.

Spots of coloured compounds are visible directly; colourless ones are located under ultraviolet light, or in a jar containing iodine crystals, or by spraying an appropriate reagent (for example ninhydrin for amino acids).

The test for halogens works on the halide ions of the sodium fusion extract, \(\text{X}^{-} + \text{Ag}^{+} \rightarrow \text{AgX}\). Nitric acid is added first for two reasons.

First, the sodium fusion extract is alkaline; acidifying it with nitric acid prevents silver ions from being precipitated as silver oxide or hydroxide instead of the silver halide.

Second, and more importantly, if nitrogen or sulphur is also present in the compound then the extract contains cyanide and sulphide ions as well. These would themselves precipitate with silver nitrate — as silver cyanide and silver sulphide — and so interfere with the test for halogens. The chapter therefore directs that the extract be boiled with concentrated nitric acid, which decomposes the cyanide and the sulphide formed during the fusion and removes them before the silver nitrate is added.

In an organic compound nitrogen, sulphur and the halogens are held by **covalent** bonds. The tests used to detect them — Prussian blue for nitrogen, lead sulphide or the nitroprusside colour for sulphur, and silver halide for the halogens — are all reactions of **ions**, and a covalently bound atom supplies no ions in solution.

Fusing the compound with metallic sodium converts these elements from the covalent form into the ionic form:

\(\text{Na} + \text{C} + \text{N} \rightarrow \text{NaCN}\)

\(2\text{Na} + \text{S} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{S}\)

\(\text{Na} + \text{X} \rightarrow \text{NaX}\) (X = Cl, Br or I)

Sodium is used because it is a highly reactive metal that reduces these elements to their anions. The cyanide, sulphide and halide of sodium so formed are water-soluble and are extracted from the fused mass by boiling it with distilled water, giving the sodium fusion extract on which the ionic tests are then carried out.

**Sublimation.**

Sublimation is the purification technique based on the fact that some solid substances change directly from the solid to the vapour state on heating, without passing through the liquid state; it is used to separate sublimable compounds from non-sublimable impurities.

Camphor is such a sublimable solid, whereas calcium sulphate is a non-volatile inorganic salt. On heating the mixture, the camphor vaporises and its vapour is condensed back to the pure solid on a cool surface, while the calcium sulphate is left behind in the dish.
_note: The chapter's section 8.8.1 states the principle of sublimation but names NO example compound, so it does not itself tell the reader that camphor sublimes; that identification is not stated in this chapter.

solution:
A liquid boils at the temperature at which its vapour pressure becomes equal to the external (atmospheric) pressure.

In steam distillation the flask contains the organic liquid together with water, and the two are immiscible, so each exerts its own vapour pressure independently of the other. The mixture therefore boils when the SUM of the two vapour pressures equals the atmospheric pressure:

\(p = p_1 + p_2\)

where \(p_1\) is the vapour pressure of the organic liquid and \(p_2\) that of water.

Since \(p_2\) is not zero, \(p_1\) is less than \(p\). The organic liquid is thus contributing only a part of the total pressure, so the temperature at which the mixture boils is lower than the temperature at which the organic liquid alone would have to reach a vapour pressure of \(p\) — that is, lower than its own boiling point. With water as the second component the mixture boils close to but below \(373\,\text{K}\).

This is why a steam-volatile, water-immiscible organic liquid vaporises at a temperature below its boiling point, and why the technique can be used for compounds that would decompose at their normal boiling points.

**No**, carbon tetrachloride will not give a white precipitate of silver chloride on heating with silver nitrate.

The silver nitrate test detects a halogen as its ION: \(\text{X}^{-} + \text{Ag}^{+} \rightarrow \text{AgX}\). In \(\text{CCl}_4\) the four chlorine atoms are joined to carbon by **covalent** bonds, so the compound does not ionise in solution and supplies no free chloride ions for the silver ion to combine with.

This is exactly why the chapter requires the compound to be fused with sodium metal before the halogen test: the fusion converts the covalently bound halogen into the ionic form \(\text{NaX}\), and only the sodium fusion extract — not the organic compound itself — gives a precipitate with silver nitrate.

In the estimation of carbon the compound is burnt in a stream of pure dry oxygen and the carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide. The mass of that carbon dioxide is what the estimation needs, and it is found from the **increase in mass** of the U-tube through which the combustion products are passed.

A solution of potassium hydroxide is used because carbon dioxide is an acidic oxide and potassium hydroxide is a strong base, so the two react completely and quantitatively:

\(2\text{KOH} + \text{CO}_2 \rightarrow \text{K}_2\text{CO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

All the carbon dioxide is therefore retained in that tube, none escapes, and the whole of the increase in the tube's mass is due to the carbon dioxide absorbed. The percentage of carbon then follows from

percentage of carbon \(= \dfrac{12 \times m_2 \times 100}{44 \times m}\)

where \(m_2\) is the mass of carbon dioxide and \(m\) the mass of the compound taken. (The water formed is absorbed separately, in a weighed U-tube of anhydrous calcium chloride placed before it.)

The lead acetate test detects sulphur as the black precipitate of lead sulphide:

\(\text{S}^{2-} + \text{Pb}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{PbS}\) (black)

Acidification is needed to release hydrogen sulphide from the sulphide of the alkaline sodium fusion extract, but the acid used must not itself react with the lead acetate reagent.

Sulphuric acid would do exactly that. Its sulphate ions give lead sulphate with lead acetate, and lead sulphate is a WHITE, insoluble precipitate. That white precipitate would appear whether or not the compound contained sulphur, would remove the lead ions needed for the real test, and would mask the black colour that the test depends on — so the result would be meaningless.

Acetic acid is used instead because it is a weak acid whose acetate ion is the same anion as in the reagent itself, so it forms no precipitate with lead ions and leaves the black lead sulphide as the only precipitate that can appear.
_note: The chapter (section 8.9.2, Test for Sulphur) PRESCRIBES acetic acid for this test but does NOT state why sulphuric acid is unsuitable. The reason given above therefore goes beyond what this chapter says, and is flagged as such.

solution:
On complete combustion all the carbon of the compound appears as carbon dioxide and all the hydrogen as water.

Mass of the compound taken, \(m = 0.20\,\text{g}\).

Mass of carbon in it \(= \dfrac{69}{100} \times 0.20 = 0.138\,\text{g}\)

Mass of hydrogen in it \(= \dfrac{4.8}{100} \times 0.20 = 0.0096\,\text{g}\)

\(12\,\text{g}\) of carbon gives \(44\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{CO}_2\), so

mass of \(\text{CO}_2 = 0.138 \times \dfrac{44}{12} = 0.506\,\text{g}\)

\(2\,\text{g}\) of hydrogen gives \(18\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\), so

mass of \(\text{H}_2\text{O} = 0.0096 \times \dfrac{18}{2} = 0.0864\,\text{g}\)

The oxygen present in the compound (\(100 - 69 - 4.8 = 26.2\%\)) does not enter either calculation.

Mass of carbon dioxide produced \(= 0.506\,\text{g}\); mass of water produced \(= 0.0864\,\text{g}\).

In Kjeldahl's method the nitrogen of the compound is converted to ammonia, which is absorbed in a known excess of standard sulphuric acid; the acid left over is found by titration with standard alkali.

Moles of \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) taken \(= 0.050\,\text{L} \times 0.5\,\text{mol L}^{-1} = 0.025\,\text{mol}\)

Moles of \(\text{NaOH}\) used \(= 0.060\,\text{L} \times 0.5\,\text{mol L}^{-1} = 0.030\,\text{mol}\)

Since \(2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\), the residual acid \(= 0.030/2 = 0.015\,\text{mol}\).

Moles of \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) neutralised by the ammonia \(= 0.025 - 0.015 = 0.010\,\text{mol}\)

Since \(2\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow (\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4\), moles of \(\text{NH}_3 = 2 \times 0.010 = 0.020\,\text{mol}\), which contain \(0.020\,\text{mol}\) of nitrogen.

Mass of nitrogen \(= 0.020 \times 14 = 0.28\,\text{g}\)

Percentage of nitrogen \(= \dfrac{0.28}{0.50} \times 100 = 56.0\%\)

In the Carius method the chlorine of the compound is precipitated quantitatively as silver chloride, and one mole of \(\text{AgCl}\) contains one mole of chlorine.

Molar mass of \(\text{AgCl} = 108 + 35.5 = 143.5\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

\(143.5\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{AgCl}\) contains \(35.5\,\text{g}\) of chlorine, so

mass of chlorine in \(0.5740\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{AgCl} = \dfrac{35.5 \times 0.5740}{143.5} = 0.1420\,\text{g}\)

Percentage of chlorine \(= \dfrac{35.5 \times 0.5740 \times 100}{143.5 \times 0.3780} = 37.57\%\)

In the Carius method for sulphur the sulphur of the compound is oxidised to sulphuric acid and precipitated as barium sulphate, and one mole of \(\text{BaSO}_4\) contains one mole of sulphur.

Molecular mass of \(\text{BaSO}_4 = 137 + 32 + 64 = 233\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

\(233\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{BaSO}_4\) contains \(32\,\text{g}\) of sulphur, so

mass of sulphur in \(0.668\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{BaSO}_4 = \dfrac{32 \times 0.668}{233} = 0.0917\,\text{g}\)

Percentage of sulphur \(= \dfrac{32 \times 0.668 \times 100}{233 \times 0.468} = 19.60\%\)
